strings.hub.priesthood.subtitle: Called, formed, ordained
strings.hub.priesthood.intro: One sacrament, two ways of living it, and the long road that leads to the laying on of hands.
strings.sec.priesthood.two_kinds.title: Religious and Diocesan Priests
strings.sec.priesthood.two_kinds.summary: Two priesthoods? No — one priesthood, lived two ways.

strings.sec.priesthood.formation.summary: From the first conversation to ordination, step by step.
strings.art.twokinds.title: Religious and Diocesan Priests
strings.art.twokinds.lead: One priesthood, two ways of living it.
strings.art.twokinds.intro: Every Catholic priest is ordained in the same sacrament of Holy Orders, and every one of them offers the same Mass. But priests belong in two different ways. A religious priest belongs to an order or congregation and professes vows in it. A diocesan priest belongs to a diocese — a place and its people — and promises obedience to its bishop. The difference is the shape of the life, not the grade of the priesthood.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.caption: Religious priest — a member of an order or congregation
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.caption: Diocesan priest — incardinated in a diocese
strings.art.twokinds.religious.belongs: A religious institute — an order or congregation, such as the Jesuits, Dominicans, Franciscans or Salesians.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.promises: Public vows of poverty, chastity and obedience — the three evangelical counsels — professed in his institute.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.obeys: His religious superior — a provincial, abbot or superior general — who assigns him.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.lives: In community, under a rule, sharing a common life and a common purse.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.work: The mission and charism of his institute: preaching, teaching, missions, care of the sick, or a life largely of prayer.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.where: Wherever his institute sends him, which may be another country or another continent.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.belongs: A diocese. He is incardinated in it — formally attached to that local Church for life.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.promises: Promises made at ordination: celibacy, and obedience and respect to his bishop. He professes no vow of poverty.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.obeys: His bishop, who appoints him to parishes and to the works of the diocese.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.lives: Usually in a parish house, alone or with one or two other priests, supported by a stipend.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.work: The care of the people of his diocese: parishes, schools, hospitals, chaplaincies and diocesan offices.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.where: Normally within his own diocese, though he may be lent to another, or sent as a missionary priest.
strings.art.twokinds.points.title: What each life asks
strings.art.twokinds.religious.1: He gives up the ownership of things: what he earns belongs to the community, which provides for him.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.2: He is formed by a charism — a particular way of following Christ, handed down from his founder.
strings.art.twokinds.religious.3: He must hold himself ready to be moved, sometimes far, when the mission requires it.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.1: He is bound to a place and its people, and usually spends his life among them.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.2: He keeps his own means and provides for himself, which brings a real duty of simplicity that no vow enforces.
strings.art.twokinds.diocesan.3: He often works without the support of a community, which is why priestly fraternity matters so much to him.
strings.art.twokinds.same.title: The same priesthood
strings.art.twokinds.same.body: Both are ordained by a bishop in the one sacrament of Holy Orders. Both consecrate the Eucharist, absolve sins, preach the Gospel, baptise, witness marriages and anoint the dying. Neither is higher than the other, and neither kind of priest can do anything at the altar that the other cannot.
strings.art.twokinds.societies.title: Not quite a straight division
strings.art.twokinds.societies.body: Between the two stand the societies of apostolic life — the Oratorians, the Vincentians, Maryknoll, the PIME missionaries — whose members live in community and share a common mission but take no religious vows. There are also secular institutes, personal prelatures and associations of diocesan priests. The two columns here are the main paths, not the only ones.
strings.art.twokinds.vows.title: A vow is not a promise
strings.art.twokinds.vows.body: A religious professes vows: promises made to God and received by the Church, which consecrate him in a state of life. A diocesan priest makes promises — celibacy at his ordination as a deacon, obedience to his bishop at both ordinations. Both bind in conscience, but they are not the same act, which is why a diocesan priest is not said to have taken vows.
strings.art.formation.title: How a Man Becomes a Priest
strings.art.formation.lead: From the first conversation to the laying on of hands.
strings.art.formation.intro: Nobody is ordained quickly. Between a man's first serious thought of priesthood and the day a bishop lays hands on him lie years of testing, study and prayer — usually seven to nine for a diocesan seminarian, and often longer for a religious. The two roads run in parallel and meet at the end, at the same altar. Choose a path to follow it stage by stage.
strings.step.dio.title: The diocesan path
strings.step.dio.intro: Formed for a diocese, by his bishop, among the people he will serve.
strings.step.dio.1.title: Discernment
strings.step.dio.1.body: It begins in prayer and in conversation — with a parish priest, a spiritual director, or the diocese's vocations director. Most dioceses run discernment evenings and “come and see” weekends long before anyone applies.
strings.step.dio.2.title: Application to the diocese
strings.step.dio.2.body: A formal application follows: interviews, references, school and work history, a medical examination and a psychological assessment. The bishop accepts the man as a seminarian of the diocese and sends him to a seminary.
strings.step.dio.3.title: The propaedeutic stage
strings.step.dio.3.body: A first year set apart for prayer, human formation and settling into the life, deliberately without academic pressure. The Church's 2016 norms made this stage obligatory everywhere; it usually lasts one to two years.
strings.step.dio.4.title: The discipleship stage — philosophy
strings.step.dio.4.body: Around two years of philosophy and the humanities, the groundwork for theology: how to think clearly, read carefully and argue honestly. Formation in prayer and community life runs alongside it.
strings.step.dio.5.title: The configuration stage — theology
strings.step.dio.5.body: Roughly four years of theology — Scripture, doctrine, moral theology, canon law, liturgy, preaching — with pastoral placements in parishes, schools, prisons and hospitals during holidays and often a full pastoral year.
strings.step.dio.6.title: Ministries and candidacy
strings.step.dio.6.body: Along the way he is instituted as a lector and then as an acolyte, and is formally admitted as a candidate for Holy Orders — the Church's public acceptance of his intention, and his of hers.
strings.step.dio.7.title: Ordination as a deacon
strings.step.dio.7.body: He is ordained a transitional deacon, usually a year before priesthood. Here he promises celibacy and obedience, takes on the daily prayer of the Church, and may preach, baptise, witness marriages and conduct funerals.
strings.step.dio.8.title: Ordination as a priest
strings.step.dio.8.body: The bishop lays hands on him in silence and prays the prayer of consecration. His hands are anointed with chrism, he is vested in stole and chasuble, and he is given the paten and chalice. From that day he can offer Mass and absolve sins.
strings.step.dio.9.title: First assignment, and formation that never ends
strings.step.dio.9.body: He is appointed to a parish, usually as an assistant, and enters what the Church calls ongoing formation: continued study, retreats and fraternity with his brother priests for the rest of his life.
strings.step.rel.title: The religious path
strings.step.rel.intro: Formed by an institute, in community, for its charism and mission.
strings.step.rel.1.title: Discernment and “come and see”
strings.step.rel.1.body: He gets to know a particular institute — its founder, its rule, its work — through visits and stays with the community. What he is discerning is twofold: priesthood, and this family in the Church.
strings.step.rel.2.title: Aspirancy or postulancy
strings.step.rel.2.body: A first period living alongside the community without yet belonging to it, from a few months to two years. He keeps its rhythm of prayer and work while both sides look honestly at the fit.
strings.step.rel.3.title: The novitiate
strings.step.rel.3.body: The heart of religious formation: at least twelve months, and often two years, given to prayer, the study of the vows and the charism, and little else. Canon law requires it, and without a valid novitiate no profession is valid.
strings.step.rel.4.title: First profession — temporary vows
strings.step.rel.4.body: He professes poverty, chastity and obedience for a set term, normally renewed over three to six years. He is now a religious, and a member of the institute, though not yet permanently bound.
strings.step.rel.5.title: Studies in philosophy and theology
strings.step.rel.5.body: The same academic road as the diocesan seminarian, usually at the institute's own house of studies or a pontifical university — but lived under vows and within the community's daily observance.
strings.step.rel.6.title: Apostolic experience
strings.step.rel.6.body: Many institutes insert a period of full-time work in their apostolate — teaching, a mission, a parish, a school — before the final stage. The Jesuits call it regency; others simply call it experience.
strings.step.rel.7.title: Perpetual profession
strings.step.rel.7.body: He professes the vows for life. In some institutes these are solemn vows, in others perpetual simple vows; either way it is the definitive gift, and it comes before ordination.
strings.step.rel.8.title: Ordination as a deacon
strings.step.rel.8.body: As on the diocesan path, he is ordained a deacon roughly a year before priesthood. He is ordained by a bishop, but presented for ordination by his own superior.
strings.step.rel.9.title: Ordination as a priest
strings.step.rel.9.body: A bishop ordains him in the same rite, with the same laying on of hands and anointing. He remains a member of his institute, and his superior — not a diocesan bishop — assigns him his work.
strings.art.formation.age.title: How old, and how long
strings.art.formation.age.body: Canon law sets the minimum ages: twenty-three for the transitional diaconate and twenty-five for priesthood. In practice men are ordained older — often in their late twenties or thirties, and second careers are common. A diocesan course usually runs seven to nine years from entry; a religious one often runs ten or more, because the novitiate and years of vows come first.
strings.art.formation.celibacy.title: Celibacy, and where it does not apply
strings.art.formation.celibacy.body: In the Latin Church a man promises celibacy at his ordination as a deacon; for a religious it is already contained in his vow of chastity. The Eastern Catholic Churches — Syro-Malabar, Maronite, Ukrainian Greek Catholic and the rest — ordain married men to the priesthood, as they have from the beginning. Celibacy is a discipline of the Latin Church, not a doctrine of the universal Church.
strings.art.formation.brothers.title: Not every religious becomes a priest
strings.art.formation.brothers.body: A man may enter a religious institute as a brother and remain one for life, and that is a complete vocation rather than a stage on the way to something else. Some institutes are entirely of brothers. A brother professes the same vows and shares the same mission; he simply is not ordained.
strings.art.formation.quote: “The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few; pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest.”
strings.sec.priesthood.leaving.title: Can a Priest Leave?
strings.sec.priesthood.leaving.summary: What can change, what never does — and why the Church's first answer is help, not the door.
strings.art.leaving.title: Can a Priest Leave the Priesthood?
strings.art.leaving.lead: What can change, and what never does.
strings.art.leaving.intro: The question is asked in two very different situations: by someone curious about how the Church works, and by a priest who is exhausted, lonely or in crisis. The short answer is that a man can be released from the duties and rights of the clerical state, but he cannot stop being a priest. And before any of that is considered, the Church's response to a priest in trouble is help — not the door.
strings.art.leaving.forever.title: Ordination cannot be undone
strings.art.leaving.forever.body: Holy Orders marks the soul with a character that is permanent. The Catechism is exact about it: a validly ordained man may be released from the obligations and functions of ordination, or forbidden to exercise them, but he cannot become a layman again in the strict sense, because that character is for ever (CCC 1583). Whatever else changes, this does not. There is no ceremony that unmakes a priest.
strings.art.leaving.first.title: Before anything else
strings.art.leaving.help.title: Most crises are not vocations ending
strings.art.leaving.help.body: Exhaustion, loneliness, depression, a loss of prayer, conflict with a bishop or a parish, the weight of scandal borne by every priest: these are reasons to ask for help, and they very often pass. The first steps are ordinary ones — telling someone honestly, a spiritual director, a doctor or counsellor, a retreat, the company of brother priests. A man in the middle of the worst year of his life is in no condition to decide the rest of it.
strings.art.leaving.leave.title: A leave of absence is not leaving
strings.art.leaving.leave.body: A bishop or superior can grant time away — months, sometimes longer — for rest, treatment or study, without any change to a priest's status. He remains a priest in good standing and may return to ministry. Many do. This is a normal pastoral provision, not a first step towards the door, and asking for it is not an admission of failure.
strings.art.leaving.ways.title: How the clerical state can be lost
strings.art.leaving.invalid.title: A declaration that the ordination was invalid
strings.art.leaving.invalid.body: If it is established that the ordination itself never took effect — because of grave defect in the man's freedom, intention or capacity at the time — a judgment or decree can declare that. This is not a release from priesthood but a finding that it was never conferred, and it is rare.
strings.art.leaving.dismissal.title: Dismissal imposed as a penalty
strings.art.leaving.dismissal.body: For grave crimes, the Church can impose dismissal from the clerical state as a penalty, through a canonical process. This is not something a priest asks for; it is done to him, and only for the gravest matters — most familiarly in cases of the abuse of minors.
strings.art.leaving.rescript.title: A rescript of the Apostolic See
strings.art.leaving.rescript.body: This is the route a priest himself can ask for. He petitions his bishop or superior, who gathers the case and sends it to Rome; only the Pope can grant it, and the law asks for grave reasons in a deacon's case and very grave reasons in a priest's. It commonly takes months, sometimes years, and it is deliberately unhurried — the delay is meant to leave room for a change of heart.
strings.art.leaving.effect.title: What a dispensation does, and does not do
strings.art.leaving.effect.1: It releases him from the obligations of the clerical state, including the daily Divine Office.
strings.art.leaving.effect.2: Dispensation from celibacy is a separate grace, and only the Pope can give it; with it, he may marry in the Church.
strings.art.leaving.effect.3: He may no longer celebrate Mass, hear confessions, preach at the liturgy, or present himself as a priest.
strings.art.leaving.effect.4: Conditions are usually attached — commonly that he not teach theology in Catholic institutions, and that he live where his past ministry will not cause upheaval.
strings.art.leaving.effect.5: It does not un-ordain him. The character remains, which is why the next point is possible at all.
strings.art.leaving.religious.title: For a religious priest
strings.art.leaving.religious.body: There are two knots, not one: the vows and the clerical state. A religious can be dispensed from his vows and leave his institute while remaining a priest — but the law will not release a religious cleric until a bishop is willing to receive him, so that no priest is left belonging nowhere.
strings.art.leaving.death.title: One thing he can always do
strings.art.leaving.death.body: A priest who has lost the clerical state — by any of the three routes above — can still validly and lawfully absolve anyone in danger of death. The Church makes no exception here, for anyone, ever. It is the clearest sign that the character is still there: the power to forgive at the last moment is never taken away.
strings.art.leaving.stay.title: Why the Church asks him to stay
strings.art.leaving.stay.body: The Church grants dispensations, and grants them mercifully, without treating the men who receive them as failures. But she asks first for perseverance, because the promise was made to God and because a parish that loses its priest loses something real. If you are a priest reading this in a hard season: tell your bishop or superior the truth about how you are, and tell someone today. That conversation has saved more vocations than any argument.
strings.art.leaving.quote: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: you are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
strings.art.leaving.hero.caption: The hardest seasons are the ones nobody sees.
strings.art.leaving.support.caption: The first step is telling someone the truth.
strings.art.leaving.religious.ref: Two knots: the vows and the clerical state
strings.art.leaving.stay.ref: Mercy, and a plea to stay
